newsitem.title: FRANCE: EU gene maize approval seen weighing on prices.
newsitem.headline: EU gene maize approval seen weighing on prices.

text.p: A European Union decision to approve gene-modified maize from the United States is likely to put pressure on maize prices by freeing up imports but leaves unanswered questions over demand for the grain, traders said.

The decision, announced by EU Farm Commission Franz Fischler in Brussels, would remove uncertainty over the fate of half a million tonnes of maize imports earmarked for Spain under a special preferential trade deal with the United States.
"This is likely to weigh down on maize prices in Europe generally because of the Spanish imports," a trader with a leading international grain company said.
Spain imports about two million tonnes of maize from the United States each year at reduced import tariffs under a 1987 deal compensating Washington for Spain's entry into the EU.

About a quarter of the 1996 quota has been left outstanding, prompting fears that it could be blocked altogether if Brussels decided not to authorise the special U.S. maize developed by Swiss company Ciba-Geigy.
Maize prices in France have been rising on such fears but were down about one percent at midday on Wednesday.
Traders said the Spanish imports would throw attention back on to the fundamentals of supply and demand, particularly a 15 percent increase in the EU maize harvest this year.
Combined with a recovery from low stocks this might give the EU a net surplus of maize, a grain in which the 15-nation bloc is usually a net importer, one trader said.
How much that knocks prices will depend on the timing, he said, though under the 1987 accord the imports should theoretically be happening fairly quickly by end-February.
"Now it is all a question of timing," one trader said.
The EU could make a decision on import tariff reductions for the next round of imports as early as Thursday, when its holds a weekly cereals committee meeting in Brussels, traders said.
Analysts and traders said there was greater uncertainty still over the reaction of maize processors to the EU decision.
Environmentalists have been trying to get the modified maize banned. And recent high-profile protests against imports of modified soybeans into Europe are fresh in everyone's minds.
"The EU may have a problem because it committed to the U.S. for a maize import quota, but what if nobody wants to take it," said Geneva-based grains consultant James Dunsterville.
On paper, at least, buying the preferential maize from the U.S. could save importers something like $50 a tonne when compared with the cost of buying maize in Europe.
But with U.S. imports likely to be spread among a large number of firms, processors might decide the gain was not worth the disruption if protests flared up, some traders said.
Animal feed manufacturers who use a lot of maize in southern Europe are seen willing to take the risk, however.

Reaction will also depend largely on what the EU means when it says the maize has been cleared with conditions on labelling, traders said. Starch manufacturers and other processors resist labelling because the raw maize itself is not segregated.
The EU Commission said on Wednesday it would soon propose improved labelling of genetically engineered food products.
Ciba-Geigy, welcoming the EU decision, acknowledged some popular resistance to the maize but a spokesman in Zurich said it would seek to address this through open information.
Initially Ciba would market the maize to farmers and not consumers, the spokesman said, adding the maize would mainly be used as a feed.
